clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive vitreoretinal degeneration caused by COL18A1 mutations affecting collagen XVIII and its endostatin fragment
Classic triad is high (often extreme) myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration with a high risk of retinal detachment, and an occipital skull defect such as an encephalocele or meningocele
Macular abnormalities and chorioretinal atrophy are common and can markedly reduce central vision
The occipital defect may be subtle (a scalp lesion or bony defect) and warrants neuroimaging when the ocular phenotype is recognised
Retinal detachment often occurs early and can be bilateral, so prophylactic surveillance is important
Cataract, lens subluxation and glaucoma may also occur
Management includes correction of high myopia, vigilant monitoring and surgical treatment of retinal detachment, neurosurgical assessment of the encephalocele, and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Knobloch syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in COL18A1, which encodes collagen XVIII, a basement-membrane collagen expressed in the eye and brain and the precursor of the anti-angiogenic fragment endostatin. Loss of functional collagen XVIII disrupts the internal limiting membrane and vitreoretinal interface, producing severe vitreoretinal degeneration, high myopia and a strong predisposition to retinal detachment. The same developmental defect in neural tissue underlies the occipital skull and meningeal defects, linking the ocular and central nervous system features.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan syndrome and other high-myopia connective tissue disorders
Walker-Warburg syndrome and other syndromic high myopia with brain malformation
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and wide-field imaging for vitreoretinal degeneration and detachment risk
Neuroimaging (MRI) to characterise the occipital encephalocele or skull defect
Optical coherence tomography for macular atrophy and vitreoretinal interface changes
Axial length and refraction to quantify high myopia
Molecular genetic testing for COL18A1 mutations
redFlags: Signs of retinal detachment (floaters, flashes, field loss) demanding urgent vitreoretinal care
An occipital scalp or skull lesion requiring neurosurgical evaluation
Rapidly progressive myopia or macular change in early childhood
Affected siblings needing screening given recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is often guarded because of high myopia, macular degeneration and recurrent retinal detachment; systemic prognosis depends on the severity of the occipital defect and any associated neurological features.
pitfalls: Missing the occipital encephalocele when it presents only as a subtle scalp or bony abnormality
Attributing the ocular picture to isolated pathological myopia and underestimating detachment risk
Failing to arrange neuroimaging once the syndrome is suspected
Not counselling parents about recessive recurrence risk
